analysis.one_liner: Requires the federal government to negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from January 2013 until the Congress ended in January 2015, never getting a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the law that bars the federal government from negotiating drug prices and instead direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, rebates, and discounts with drug manufacturers for Medicare's Part D prescription drug benefit. The prices would apply to the private drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that serve Medicare beneficiaries, while plans could still negotiate even lower prices. It was introduced in January 2013, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans, who would benefit from lower negotiated drug prices, which could translate into lower premiums and lower out-of-pocket drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the statutory 'noninterference' provision and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers the prices, discounts, and rebates that may be charged to Part D drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations for covered Part D drugs.

Plans could still obtain discounts below the HHS-negotiated price, so the provision does not cap savings, and the Secretary would have to report to Congress every six months on the prices and discounts achieved.
The negotiated prices were to apply starting with plan years beginning January 1, 2014.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a single large buyer bargaining down Medicare drug prices, reducing revenue on a major block of sales. Taxpayers could also benefit through lower government subsidies, while manufacturers' reduced revenue is the cost the bill is designed to impose.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly bars the Secretary from establishing or requiring a particular formulary, which critics argue removes the main bargaining lever other public buyers use; without the threat of excluding drugs from coverage, negotiation may yield smaller savings than advocates expect.
A single federal negotiation process could reduce the price competition among multiple Part D plans that some economists credit with holding down Part D costs under the current system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit runs to Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers through lower drug prices, and the main cost falls on drug manufacturers. The bill's design limitation—negotiation without formulary authority—means the savings may be more modest than the strongest versions of this idea, but the core change shifts bargaining power from manufacturers toward the largest drug buyer in the country.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2013 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Price Negotiation Act on January 23, 2013, with five original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance that same day; that referral was the last action ever taken on the bill in the 113th Congress.
The bill accumulated eight cosponsors (6 Democrats, 2 Independents) but never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices remained in place for the rest of the 113th Congress, and Medicare kept paying prices set without direct federal negotiation. Beneficiaries and taxpayers, who would have shared the savings, did not.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 23, 2013, directing HHS to negotiate Medicare Part D drug prices.

for.name: Sens. Begich, Franken, Johnson (SD), Sanders, and Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 8 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 2 Independents)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill over the course of the 113th Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in January 2013 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry that would bear the bill's cost
against.what_they_did: Opposed giving the federal government negotiating authority over Medicare drug prices, a position the industry has consistently taken since the Part D benefit was created with a statutory bar on federal negotiation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill's only movement was a referral to the Finance Committee chaired by a member of the president's own party, after which nothing happened.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to sell to Medicare at prices, rebates, and discounts negotiated by HHS rather than at prices bargained privately with competing drug plans. Their interest in killing the bill ran directly against beneficiaries and taxpayers who would have shared the savings.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations would buy drugs at lower HHS-negotiated prices, cutting their input costs, but they would lose their current role as the sole price negotiators with manufacturers. They could still seek discounts below the negotiated price.
